questions.prompt: A plain Newton direction can fail to be a descent direction when
options: the step length is shortened below \(1\)
the objective is a positive definite quadratic
the Hessian is not positive definite
the Hessian is positive definite and the gradient is not zero
questions.explanation: The directional derivative of a Newton step is \(-g^T H^{-1} g\) only when \(H\) is invertible, and that quantity is negative for every nonzero \(g\) when \(H\) is positive definite. If \(H\) has a negative eigenvalue, the same formula can be positive, so the step climbs. Shortening a length cannot repair a direction that climbs: every positive length still increases the model. A positive definite quadratic is the case where the plain Newton step is a descent step and lands on the minimizer.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: At a point where the derivative is \(6\) and the second derivative is \(-2\), a shift \(\mu = 6\) is added before the Newton equation. What is the shifted step?
questions.explanation: The shifted curvature is \(-2 + 6 = 4\). The equation is \(4 d = -6\), so \(d = -3/2\). The unshifted equation \(-2 d = -6\) gives \(d = 3\), which has a positive directional derivative \(6 \cdot 3 = 18\) and is not the shifted step. Reporting \(3/2\) drops the minus sign. Reporting \(4\) is the shifted curvature.

options: subtract a positive multiple of the identity so the Hessian becomes indefinite
keep a descent direction and shorten the trial length until a sufficient-decrease test accepts it
replace the gradient by zero and skip the solve
take the full Newton step even when the objective increases
questions.explanation: Damping here is a line search on a direction that is already descent. A rejected length is replaced by a shorter one until sufficient decrease holds. Replacing the gradient by zero removes the right-hand side. Taking a full step that increases the objective is the failure damping is meant to avoid. A positive shift is added to the Hessian, not subtracted. Subtracting would push eigenvalues down.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The Hessian at the current point is not positive definite. Put the steps of one shifted, damped Newton iteration in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The shift is chosen from the Hessian that was just evaluated, so the evaluation comes first. The linear system uses the shifted matrix, so the shift comes before the solve. The trial length is a scalar along the direction that the solve produced. The point moves only after a length has been accepted. Accepting and rejecting are not separate branches in this list: shortening until acceptance is one step, and it has to finish before the move.

steps: Evaluate the gradient and the Hessian at the current point.
Add a positive multiple of the identity large enough that the shifted Hessian is positive definite.
Solve the shifted linear system for the direction.
Shorten the trial length by repeated factors in \((0, 1)\) until the Armijo inequality accepts it.
Move the point by the accepted length times that direction.

questions.prompt: The second derivative is \(-2\). Which shifts \(\mu\) make the shifted curvature \(-2 + \mu\) positive?
questions.explanation:
Positive definite curvature in one variable is a positive number, not zero.
• \(\mu = 1\) leaves \(-1\), which is negative.
• \(\mu = 3\) leaves \(1\), which is positive.
• \(\mu = 2\) leaves \(0\). A zero curvature is singular, so the shifted Newton equation does not determine a step.
• \(\mu = 6\) leaves \(4\), which is positive.

questions.prompt: A scalar derivative \(g\), second derivative \(h\), and shift \(m\) produce the shifted Newton step
questions.explanation: The shifted equation is \((h+m) d = -g\). The ranges keep \(h+m\) positive, so there is one step, \(d = -g/(h+m)\). Every declared name appears. Using \(-g/h\) ignores the shift. Using \(-g/(h-m)\) subtracts the shift and can destroy the positive curvature the shift was added to create. Using \((h+m)/g\) inverts the equation.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a column of two labels</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">p</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">q</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A note shifts a second derivative of \(-3\) by \(\mu = 1\), with derivative \(4\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The shifted curvature is \(-2\), and \(-2 d = -4\) does give \(d = 2\). The product of the derivative and that step is \(8\), which is positive, so the objective increases to first order. A descent direction would need a negative directional derivative. The last claim is true: \(-3 + \mu > 0\) forces \(\mu > 3\). The shift \(1\) is too small.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.
steps: The directional derivative \(4 \cdot 2 = 8\) is negative, so the direction is a descent direction.
The curvature stays nonpositive until the shift is larger than \(3\).
reasons: The product \(4 \cdot 2\) equals \(8\), which is positive, so the direction is not descent.
The equation \(-2 d = -4\) does not give \(d = 2\).

questions.prompt: The derivative is \(4\), the second derivative is \(-3\), and the shift is \(\mu = 5\). What is the directional derivative along the shifted Newton step?
questions.explanation: The shifted curvature is \(-3 + 5 = 2\). Then \(2 d = -4\), so \(d = -2\). The directional derivative is \(4 \cdot (-2) = -8\). The negative sign says the shifted step is a descent direction. Reporting \(8\) drops that sign. Reporting \(-2\) is the step. Reporting \(2\) is the shifted curvature. With the too-small shift \(\mu = 1\), the step would be \(2\) and the directional derivative would be \(8\), which is the quantity this shift avoids.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Once a shifted Newton direction is a descent direction, Armijo backtracking
options: replaces a rejected length \(t\) by \(\beta t\) with \(\beta \in (0, 1)\)
doubles the length until the objective increases
flips the sign of the direction after every rejected trial
removes the shift before the first trial
questions.explanation: Backtracking starts from a trial length and multiplies it by a fixed factor in \((0, 1)\) whenever the sufficient-decrease inequality fails. A descent direction guarantees that a short enough trial passes. Doubling the length goes the other way. Flipping the sign turns a descent direction into an ascent direction. The shift is what made the direction a descent direction, so it stays in place during the line search.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: A later method takes a Newton step in a scaled metric and then projects the result onto a convex set. That method is
options: a simplex ratio test on a linear program
a power iteration that ignores the feasible set
an exact line search along a coordinate axis with no projection
a scaled projected step, with the ordinary projected gradient recovered when the scaling is the identity
questions.explanation: Scaling by a positive definite matrix, such as a shifted Hessian, changes the metric of the step. Projecting in that metric keeps the next point feasible. When the scaling is the identity, the step is an ordinary gradient step before the projection. A simplex ratio test chooses a step that stays nonnegative in a linear program, without a Newton metric. Power iteration looks for an eigenvector. An exact line search on an axis does not project a Newton step.

questions.prompt: The Hessian is diagonal with entries \(-1\) and \(4\). What is the smallest positive integer shift \(\mu\) that makes this Hessian plus \(\mu I\) positive definite?
questions.explanation: The shifted eigenvalues are \(-1 + \mu\) and \(4 + \mu\). Both are positive only when \(\mu > 1\). The smallest positive integer with that property is \(2\): the eigenvalues are then \(1\) and \(6\). The shift \(1\) leaves a zero eigenvalue, which is singular rather than positive definite. The shift \(4\) also works, but it is not the smallest positive integer. Reporting \(-1\) is an eigenvalue of the unshifted matrix.

questions.prompt: A later root iteration solves a perturbed complementarity system by Newton steps that are kept inside the positive region. That iteration is
options: a line search that refuses every positive length
a shift that makes the Hessian singular on purpose
a primal-dual interior step on the perturbed system
a projected gradient step with no linear solve
questions.explanation: The perturbed system is a set of nonlinear equations, one block of them from complementarity. A Newton step linearizes that system, and the step is controlled so the iterates stay positive. That is an interior method. A projected gradient step does not solve the perturbed Jacobian system. Refusing every positive length stalls. A shift that creates a zero eigenvalue removes the Newton step instead of keeping it inside the region.
